cards.front: MCV (fL) is calculated from [[1]] divided by [[2]]; MCHC is calculated from hemoglobin divided by hematocrit.
cards.back: 1: hematocrit  2: red cell count

cards.front: What does an elevated RDW indicate?
cards.back: Anisocytosis — a mixed or evolving red cell population (e.g., developing iron deficiency); thalassemia trait typically has a normal RDW.

cards.front: What is EDTA pseudothrombocytopenia and how is it resolved?
cards.back: EDTA-dependent platelet clumping causing a falsely low count; the smear shows clumps and recollection in citrate (or another anticoagulant) resolves it.

cards.front: Classic adult teaching cutoffs: microcytic MCV below about [[1]] fL; macrocytic MCV above about [[2]] fL (verify local intervals).
cards.note: Pediatric and neonatal intervals differ by age.

cards.front: How do you correct the white cell count for nucleated red cells?
cards.back: Corrected WBC = measured WBC x 100 / (100 + nRBC per 100 WBC).

cards.front: What is the purpose of analyzer flags and histograms?
cards.back: Quality assurance: they mark events the analyzer cannot classify reliably and route the specimen to manual smear review; they are not diagnoses.

cards.front: How can giant platelets cause a falsely low automated platelet count?
cards.back: Impedance counting classifies by volume; giant platelets may be counted as small red cells. Optical/fluorescent counts and smear estimation resolve the discrepancy.

cards.front: The reticulocyte production index corrects for the degree of [[1]] and reticulocyte [[2]] time.
cards.back: 1: anemia  2: maturation

cards.front: What does a dimorphic red cell histogram suggest?
cards.back: Two red cell populations — recent transfusion, dual deficiency, or sideroblastic process; always take a transfusion history.

cards.front: Name the toxic neutrophil changes seen in severe infection.
cards.back: Toxic granulation, Dohle bodies, and cytoplasmic vacuolization (plus a left shift with band forms).

cards.front: Iron deficiency pattern: ferritin [[1]], serum iron low, TIBC [[2]], transferrin saturation low.
cards.back: 1: low  2: high

cards.front: Why can ferritin be normal in iron deficiency?
cards.back: Ferritin is an acute-phase reactant; inflammation, infection, or liver disease can raise it despite depleted stores. Soluble transferrin receptor helps in such cases.

cards.front: How does anemia of chronic disease differ from iron deficiency on iron studies?
cards.back: ACD: low iron, low TIBC, normal/high ferritin (iron sequestration). Iron deficiency: low iron, high TIBC, low ferritin.

cards.front: Beta-thalassemia trait shows [[1]] HbA2 on hemoglobin analysis; alpha-thalassemia trait usually has a [[2]] HbA2.
cards.back: 1: elevated  2: normal

cards.front: Which marker is elevated specifically in vitamin B12 deficiency but not folate deficiency?
cards.back: Methylmalonic acid (homocysteine is elevated in both).

cards.front: List the hemolysis laboratory panel.
cards.back: Reticulocyte count/RPI up, haptoglobin down, LDH up, indirect bilirubin up, plus smear and DAT; hemoglobinuria/hemosiderinuria in intravascular hemolysis.

cards.front: Schistocytes with thrombocytopenia and a [[1]] DAT suggest microangiopathic hemolysis; spherocytes with a [[2]] DAT suggest warm AIHA.
cards.back: 1: negative  2: positive

cards.front: What does a solubility screening test detect, and what are its limitations?
cards.back: It detects HbS presence (positive in trait and disease) but cannot distinguish them and does not detect other variants; confirm with electrophoresis/HPLC.

cards.front: Which findings favor thalassemia trait over iron deficiency in microcytosis?
cards.back: Normal RDW, normal/high ferritin, normal TIBC, and a red cell count relatively high for the degree of anemia; often target cells on smear.

cards.front: What megaloblastic changes appear on the peripheral smear?
cards.back: Macro-ovalocytes, hypersegmented neutrophils (5 or more lobes), and megaloblastic marrow changes.

cards.front: PT/INR evaluates the [[1]] and common pathways; aPTT evaluates the [[2]] and common pathways.
cards.back: 1: extrinsic  2: intrinsic

cards.front: What does an isolated prolonged PT suggest?
cards.back: Factor VII deficiency (or warfarin effect / early liver disease) — the extrinsic pathway with short-half-life factor VII.

cards.front: How does a mixing study distinguish factor deficiency from an inhibitor?
cards.back: 1:1 mix with normal pooled plasma: immediate correction = factor deficiency; failure to correct = inhibitor (heparin, lupus anticoagulant, specific factor inhibitor).

cards.front: A time-dependent inhibitor that worsens with incubation is classically an anti-[[1]] antibody; lupus anticoagulant paradoxically increases [[2]] risk.
cards.back: 1: FVIII (factor VIII)  2: thrombosis (clotting)

cards.front: Which test is most sensitive to heparin contamination?
cards.back: Thrombin time (TT) — markedly prolonged by even small heparin amounts.

cards.front: What is the typical INR therapeutic target for warfarin in most indications?
cards.back: 2.0 to 3.0 (higher ranges for some mechanical valves); targets are guideline and indication dependent — verify locally.

cards.front: DIC labs: PT/aPTT [[1]], platelets low, fibrinogen low (may be [[2]] early as an acute-phase reactant), D-dimer high, schistocytes present.
cards.back: 1: prolonged  2: normal

cards.front: Why does an underfilled citrate tube falsely prolong PT and aPTT?
cards.back: Excess citrate relative to the 1:9 blood ratio is not fully neutralized by calcium in the test, delaying clot formation; recollect in a properly filled tube.

cards.front: What is the citrate adjustment rule for very high hematocrit?
cards.back: When hematocrit exceeds roughly 55 percent, the citrate volume must be reduced per protocol to maintain the 1:9 anticoagulant-to-blood ratio.

cards.front: Which deficiency causes bleeding with completely normal PT and aPTT?
cards.back: Factor XIII deficiency (fibrin stabilization defect); also mild von Willebrand disease may screen normal.

cards.front: Warfarin is monitored by [[1]]; unfractionated heparin is monitored by [[2]] or anti-Xa.
cards.back: 1: INR  2: aPTT

cards.front: How are direct factor Xa inhibitors (apixaban, rivaroxaban) quantified when needed?
cards.back: With drug-calibrated anti-factor Xa assays; routine monitoring is not required, but assays help in bleeding, renal failure, and reversal decisions.

cards.front: Which assay monitors dabigatran effect?
cards.back: Dilute thrombin time (or ecarin clotting time); dabigatran is a direct thrombin inhibitor.

cards.front: What are the classic clinical features distinguishing primary from secondary hemostasis defects?
cards.back: Primary (platelet/vessel): mucocutaneous bleeding — petechiae, purpura, epistaxis. Secondary (coagulation): deep tissue bleeding — hemarthroses, intramuscular hematomas.

cards.front: vWF mediates platelet adhesion by binding [[1]] to collagen; fibrinogen bridges platelets via [[2]] during aggregation.
cards.back: 1: GPIb (glycoprotein Ib)  2: GPIIb/IIIa (glycoprotein IIb/IIIa)

cards.front: Why is lupus anticoagulant testing difficult on warfarin?
cards.back: Warfarin lowers vitamin K-dependent factors and interferes with phospholipid-dependent assays used for lupus anticoagulant detection.

cards.front: What is the role of anti-Xa monitoring for low molecular weight heparin?
cards.back: Reserved for special populations (renal failure, obesity, pregnancy, pediatrics), typically measured at peak after dosing; routine monitoring is not standard.

cards.front: D-dimer is elevated in DIC and thrombosis but is [[1]]; it also rises in [[2]], inflammation, and pregnancy.
cards.back: 1: nonspecific (sensitive but nonspecific)  2: malignancy (or surgery/trauma)

cards.front: What is the laboratory picture of early DIC?
cards.back: Mildly prolonged PT/aPTT, falling platelets, D-dimer rising; fibrinogen may still be normal as an acute-phase reactant — trend the panel.

cards.front: What are the reversal agents for common anticoagulants?
cards.back: Warfarin: vitamin K plus prothrombin complex concentrate. Heparin: protamine. Dabigatran: idarucizumab. Factor Xa inhibitors: andexanet alfa or PCC per guidelines.
